```{r setup}
library(energyRt)
library(ggplot2)
```

# One object, many processes

A technology is rarely one thing. A gas plant built in 2025 is not the plant you
build in 2035: it costs more and burns more fuel for the same electricity. Wind
is not one resource but a handful of site grades, the best ones finite. A
transmission corridor is not one line but a stack of tranches, each with its own
losses.

energyRt writes all three with the same mechanism. One object declares a
**family**, and at interpolation it is **expanded** into one ordinary process per
member -- so the solver sees plain processes and every equation stays as it is.
The family has two axes:

| axis | slot | what a member is | ordered? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **vintage** | `@vintage` | a build year, with its own costs and efficiency | yes, by year |
| **cluster** | `@cluster` | a parallel part that exists *at the same time* as its siblings | only by convention (`order`) |

The distinction is worth getting right at the start: **vintages are sequential,
clusters are simultaneous**. Vintages differ in *when* they were built; clusters
differ in *what* they are -- a grade, a site class, a tranche, a fleet type.

A member's name carries its provenance, so solver output, reports and levies all
refer to something you can read:

```
PP   + vintage 2035                  -> PP_VIN2035
EWIN + cluster 01                    -> EWIN_CL01
ECOA + vintage 2030 + cluster CCS    -> ECOA_VIN2030_CLCCS
```

The prefixes are model-wide settings (`_VIN` and `_CL` by default), since they
become solver set-member names:

```{r prefix, eval = FALSE}
mod <- newModel(name = "m", variant_prefix = c(cluster = "_T"))  # EWIN_T01
```

**Cluster labels are zero-padded ordinals** (`"01"`, `"02"`, ...) for resource
tiers. Two reasons: the same token then ties every object of one tier together
(`WWIN_CL01`, `LAND_CL01`, `RES_LAND_CL01`, `EWIN_VIN2040_CL01`), and 40 tiers
sort `01..40` instead of `1, 10, 11, 2`. What a tier *means* goes in `desc`,
where it cannot be parsed back out of a name by mistake.

Every example below is a complete model you can paste and run, written out in
full rather than wrapped in a helper, so each one stands alone. Each carries a
deliberately expensive `newImport()` as a backstop: it is never used in the
solutions shown, and it is there so the examples stay feasible if you change a
bound while reading.

```{r calendar}
cal <- newCalendar(
  timetable = make_timetable(
    struct = list(ANNUAL = "ANNUAL", SEASON = c("WIN", "SUM"))),
  name = "two_seasons")
```

# Vintages: the same plant, built later

`@vintage` declares the build years a technology comes in, and the other slots
carry a `vintage` column saying which member a row belongs to. Here the 2035
vintage is cheaper to build *and* more efficient -- the ordinary case for any
technology still on a learning curve:

```{r vintage-def}
PP <- newTechnology(
  name = "PP",
  desc = "Gas plant, two build vintages",
  input = data.frame(comm = "GAS", unit = "PJ"),
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  vintage = data.frame(
    vintage = c("2025", "2035"),
    start   = c(2025, 2035),   # first year this vintage may be BUILT
    end     = 2050,            # last year it may be built
    olife   = 30L              # operational life, once built
  ),
  ceff = data.frame(
    vintage = c("2025", "2035"),
    comm = "ELC",
    cact2cout = c(0.40, 0.55)  # GWh out per GWh of fuel in
  ),
  invcost = data.frame(
    vintage = c("2025", "2035"),
    invcost = c(1200, 900)     # MUSD/GW
  ),
  capacity = data.frame(cap.up = 400),  # GW; no vintage column: both members
  cap2act = 8.76                        # GW -> GWh/year
)
```

Three things in that declaration are worth naming.

`start`/`end` are an **investment window**, not a lifetime: they say when the
vintage may be *built*, while `olife` says how long it then runs. The windows may
overlap, as they do here -- from 2035 both vintages are buildable and the model
chooses.

`capacity` carries **no** `vintage` column, so its row applies to every member.
That is the general rule for every slot: a selector column left `NA` broadcasts
to all variants, so you name a vintage only where the members actually differ.

Units are stated on both flows and the conversion is explicit: `cap2act = 8.76`
turns a capacity in GW into GWh per year, so `invcost` reads MUSD/GW and the
levelized costs later in this article come out in USD/MWh.

```{r vintage-model}
GAS <- newCommodity(name = "GAS", timeframe = "ANNUAL", unit = "PJ")
ELC <- newCommodity(name = "ELC", timeframe = "SEASON", unit = "GWh")

SUP_GAS <- newSupply(
  name = "SUP_GAS",
  commodity = "GAS",
  supply = data.frame(cost = 4)   # MUSD/PJ
)
IMP_ELC <- newImport(
  name = "IMP_ELC",
  commodity = "ELC",
  import = data.frame(price = 5000)  # backstop, never economic
)
DEM_GROW <- newDemand(
  name = "DEM_ELC",
  commodity = "ELC",
  demand = data.frame(year = c(2025, 2050), demand = c(18, 30))  # GWh/slice
)

repo_vin <- newRepository(
  name = "repo_vin",
  GAS, ELC, SUP_GAS, IMP_ELC, DEM_GROW, PP
)
mod_vin <- newModel(
  name = "art_vintage",
  repo = repo_vin,
  calendar = cal,
  region = "R1",
  horizon = newHorizon(seq(2025, 2050, by = 5)),
  discount = 0.05
)
scen_vin <- solve_model(
  obj = mod_vin,
  name = "art_vintage",
  ondisk = FALSE,
  overwrite = TRUE,
  echo = FALSE
)
getVariants(scen_vin)
```

`getVariants()` is the provenance table: every expanded process, its class, the
object it came from, and its coordinates on the two axes. It is the map between
what you declared and what the solver saw.

Now the investment decision itself:

```{r vintage-build}
newcap <- getData(scen_vin, name = "vTechNewCap", merge = TRUE)
newcap <- as.data.frame(newcap)
built <- newcap[newcap$value > 1e-6, c("tech", "year", "value")]
head(built, 8)   # GW
```

The 2025 vintage builds 90 GW up front and tops up as demand grows; from 2035
every addition is the newer vintage, because it is both cheaper and more
efficient. Nothing retires mid-horizon and the backstop stays idle -- the whole
story is "which vintage gets the next increment".

To report per axis rather than per process, `variantSummary()` folds the members
back along the axis you ask for:

```{r vintage-summary}
vs <- variantSummary(
  scen = scen_vin,
  name = "vTechNewCap",
  by = "vintage"
)
head(as.data.frame(vs), 4)
```

It returns `n`, `total`, `mean`, `sd`, `min` and `max` per group rather than a
bare `value`, because a family is a set and "the" value of a set is a choice you
should make explicitly.

# Clusters: parallel parts of one family

A cluster member exists *alongside* its siblings. The canonical case is a
resource in grades: the best wind sites are cheap and few, the poor ones are
plentiful and expensive, and each grade has its own ceiling.

```{r cluster-def}
EWIN <- newTechnology(
  name = "EWIN",
  desc = "Wind, three site grades",
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  cluster = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    desc    = c("best sites", "average", "leftovers"),
    region  = NA_character_,   # all three exist everywhere
    order   = 1:3              # reporting order, best first
  ),
  af = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    af.up = c(0.45, 0.33, 0.22)    # capacity factor by grade
  ),
  capacity = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    cap.up = c(8, 16, 40)          # GW of potential by grade
  ),
  invcost = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    invcost = c(600, 900, 1800)    # MUSD/GW
  ),
  fixom = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    fixom = c(20, 22, 25)          # MUSD/GW/year
  ),
  vintage = data.frame(olife = 25L),
  cap2act = 8.76
)
```

Each grade carries its own availability factor, its own potential (`cap.up`) and
its own cost. Put it next to a gas plant and let the model choose:

```{r cluster-model}
PP_flat <- newTechnology(
  name = "PP_flat",
  input = data.frame(comm = "GAS", unit = "PJ"),
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  ceff = data.frame(comm = "ELC", cact2cout = 0.4),
  invcost = data.frame(invcost = 1200),
  capacity = data.frame(cap.up = 400),
  vintage = data.frame(olife = 30L),
  cap2act = 8.76
)
DEM_FLAT <- newDemand(
  name = "DEM_ELC",
  commodity = "ELC",
  demand = data.frame(demand = 18)   # GWh/slice, flat over the horizon
)

repo_clu <- newRepository(
  name = "repo_clu",
  GAS, ELC, SUP_GAS, IMP_ELC, DEM_FLAT, PP_flat, EWIN
)
mod_clu <- newModel(
  name = "art_cluster",
  repo = repo_clu,
  calendar = cal,
  region = "R1",
  horizon = newHorizon(seq(2025, 2040, by = 5)),
  discount = 0.05
)
scen_clu <- solve_model(
  obj = mod_clu,
  name = "art_cluster",
  ondisk = FALSE,
  overwrite = TRUE,
  echo = FALSE
)

cap <- getData(scen_clu, name = "vTechCap", merge = TRUE)
cap <- as.data.frame(cap)
cap[cap$year == 2025 & grepl("EWIN", cap$tech), c("tech", "value")]   # GW
```

The best grade is built to its ceiling (8 GW), the average one likewise (16 GW),
and the poor grade is left in the ground -- its 40 GW of potential are not worth
having at 1800 MUSD/GW. That is the point of a graded resource: a single average
cost would have built either too much or too little.

## Clusters that differ by region

`@cluster`'s `region` column scopes a member, and it is intersected with the
object's own `region`. This is how a tier set of a *different size* in each
region is expressed -- the usual situation for land or wind resources:

```{r cluster-region}
EWIN_R <- newTechnology(
  name = "EWIN",
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  cluster = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02"),
    region = c(NA, "R1")    # grade 02 exists in R1 only
  ),
  af = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), af.up = c(0.45, 0.33)),
  capacity = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), cap.up = 10),
  invcost = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), invcost = c(600, 900)),
  vintage = data.frame(olife = 25L),
  cap2act = 8.76
)
DEM_SMALL <- newDemand(
  name = "DEM_ELC",
  commodity = "ELC",
  demand = data.frame(demand = 6)
)

repo_rr <- newRepository(
  name = "repo_rr",
  GAS, ELC, SUP_GAS, IMP_ELC, DEM_SMALL, PP_flat, EWIN_R
)
mod_rr <- newModel(
  name = "art_region",
  repo = repo_rr,
  calendar = cal,
  region = c("R1", "R2"),
  horizon = newHorizon(c(2025, 2030)),
  discount = 0.05
)
scen_rr <- interpolate_model(mod_rr, name = "art_region", ondisk = FALSE)

# any per-process input parameter shows which variants exist where, and
# `getData()` adds the provenance columns
inv <- getData(scen_rr, name = "pTechInvcost", merge = TRUE)
inv <- as.data.frame(inv)
unique(inv[, c("tech", "region", "cluster")])
```

`EWIN_CL01` exists in both regions and `EWIN_CL02` only in R1 -- three
`(process, region)` cells from one object, not four. A cluster whose regions do
not overlap the object's own is an error rather than an empty process.

A region-scoped declaration carries one row per `(cluster, region)`, so a member
existing in four regions keeps four rows. The **label** identifies the member;
the row count does not.

## Shares: two different levers

Two groups of columns on `@cluster` bound how a family splits, and they are *not*
alternatives:

| column | what it ties | typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `cap.share.fx` | the ratio of members' **capacities**, every year | loss tranches, where each tranche's efficiency is calibrated to its place in the stack |
| `act.share.lo/up/fx` | a member's share of the family's **throughput** | stopping a family collapsing onto its cheapest member |

Both are optional: a member with neither sizes and runs freely, as the wind
grades above do. Some classes deliberately have **no** `cap.share.fx` at all --
`supply`, `demand`, `import` and `export` have no capacity variable for it to
act on, so the column is absent rather than present-and-ignored, and the mistake
is rejected when you build the object instead of silently doing nothing.

# Seeing a family

`draw()` sketches one object's flow structure, which for a clustered technology
is the structure every member shares:

```{r draw, fig.height = 3}
draw(EWIN)
```

`autoplot()` on a process plots its declared data rather than its structure, so
the per-grade differences show up directly:

```{r autoplot-tech}
autoplot(EWIN)
```

On a solved scenario `autoplot()` takes `by = "cluster"` (or `"vintage"`), which
is the reason members carry a provenance label at all:

```{r autoplot-scen}
autoplot(
  object = scen_clu,
  type = "capacity",
  comm = "ELC",
  by = "cluster"
)
```

# Levelized cost per member

The build order above -- grade 01 to its ceiling, then 02, never 03 -- is an
outcome of the solve. `levcost()` shows the *cause*, and it needs no model at
all: a technology plus its own costs is enough for a closed-form LCOE.

```{r levcost-table}
lc <- levcost(
  object = EWIN,
  by_variant = TRUE
)
lc <- as.data.frame(lc)
lc[lc$year == 2030, c("variant", "cluster", "comm", "levcost")]   # USD/MWh
```

The ordering is the whole explanation: grade 01 is the cheapest electricity in
the model, 02 is worth building once 01 is exhausted, and 03 at roughly five
times the cost of 01 never competes with a 1200 MUSD/GW gas plant. The cluster
declaration and the solved result are two views of one ranking.

Without `by_variant` the result keeps its class and plots directly, one series
per member:

```{r levcost-plot}
lc_obj <- levcost(object = EWIN)
autoplot(lc_obj)
```

A vintaged technology works the same way, which is how you see a learning curve
before solving anything:

```{r levcost-vintage}
lc_pp <- levcost(
  object = PP,
  by_variant = TRUE
)
lc_pp <- as.data.frame(lc_pp)
lc_pp[lc_pp$year == 2040, c("variant", "vintage", "comm", "levcost")]
```

# The two axes together

A technology may carry both, and expansion takes the grid: one process per
`(vintage, cluster)` cell.

```{r grid, eval = FALSE}
ECOA <- newTechnology(
  name = "ECOA",
  input = data.frame(comm = "COA", unit = "PJ"),
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  vintage = data.frame(
    vintage = c("2025", "2035"),
    start = c(2025, 2035),
    end = 2050,
    olife = 40L
  ),
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("PLAIN", "CCS")),
  # a row may select on either axis; NA broadcasts over that axis
  ceff = data.frame(
    vintage = c(NA, NA, "2035"),
    cluster = c("PLAIN", "CCS", "CCS"),
    comm = "ELC",
    cact2cout = c(0.42, 0.33, 0.36)   # CCS improves in the 2035 vintage
  ),
  invcost = data.frame(invcost = 1500),
  cap2act = 8.76
)
# -> ECOA_VIN2025_CLPLAIN, ECOA_VIN2025_CLCCS,
#    ECOA_VIN2035_CLPLAIN, ECOA_VIN2035_CLCCS
```

Two rules make these tables readable:

* an `NA` in a selector column **broadcasts** to every member on that axis, so
  you write a row once and override it only where a member differs;
* a row whose selector is the literal `"TOTAL"` is not a member at all -- it is a
  bound on the *family*, which becomes a constraint across the expanded
  processes rather than data on one of them.

A cluster label here is a *kind* (`PLAIN`, `CCS`), not a resource tier, so the
ordinal convention does not apply: nothing else in the model carries the token.

# Clustered resources: tiers that must not pool

Grades on a *process* get you most of the way, but two things sit outside the
process and need the same treatment.

## Weather tiers

A graded wind resource usually has a different **profile** per grade, not just a
different ceiling. Declare the tiers on the `weather` object and keep one object
for the whole set:

```{r weather-tiers}
WWIN <- newWeather(
  name = "WWIN",
  desc = "Wind capacity factor by site grade",
  timeframe = "SEASON",
  unit = "share",
  cluster = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02"),
    desc = c("good sites", "poor sites"),
    region = NA_character_,
    order = 1:2
  ),
  weather = data.frame(
    cluster   = rep(c("01", "02"), each = 2),
    region    = "R1",
    year      = 2025L,
    timeslice = rep(c("WIN", "SUM"), 2),
    wval      = c(0.9, 0.6,   0.45, 0.3)
  )
)

EWIN_W <- newTechnology(
  name = "EWIN",
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), region = NA_character_),
  capacity = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), cap.up = 10),
  invcost = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), invcost = 600),
  # ONE link row per tier, each naming the same object
  weather = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02"),
    weather = "WWIN",
    waf.up = 1
  ),
  vintage = data.frame(olife = 25L),
  cap2act = 8.76
)

repo_w <- newRepository(
  name = "repo_w",
  GAS, ELC, SUP_GAS, IMP_ELC, DEM_SMALL, PP_flat, WWIN, EWIN_W
)
mod_w <- newModel(
  name = "art_weather",
  repo = repo_w,
  calendar = cal,
  region = "R1",
  horizon = newHorizon(c(2025, 2030)),
  discount = 0.05
)
scen_w <- interpolate_model(mod_w, name = "art_weather", ondisk = FALSE)

pw <- getData(scen_w, name = "pWeather", merge = TRUE)
unique(as.data.frame(pw)$weather)
```

Each tier became an ordinary weather object, `WWIN_CL01` and `WWIN_CL02`, and
the process variants read one each:

```{r weather-link}
link <- getData(scen_w, name = "pTechWeatherAf", merge = TRUE)
link <- as.data.frame(link)
unique(link[, c("tech", "weather", "cluster")])
```

A consumer finds its tier **by cluster name** -- the reason the label is built
once and shared. A link row carrying `cluster = "01"` reads the `01` rows; a link
to an *unclustered* weather object is untouched (so a single shared profile keeps
working exactly as before); and a link to a clustered object with no cluster is
an error, because a multiplicative factor has no "every tier at once" reading.
Tiers compose with `transform`, giving `WWIN_CL01_<transform>`: the cluster picks
the series, the transform derives from it.

## Commodity tiers, and why they are needed

Now the harder half. Suppose each wind grade needs **land**, and land is finite
per grade. The obvious move -- one `LAND` commodity, one supply object with three
clusters -- does *not* bind per grade:

> The commodity balance is keyed on `(comm, region, year, timeslice)` and carries
> no cluster. Every producer of one commodity *name* writes into the same cell,
> so three supply clusters pour into one pool and grade-01 wind can draw
> grade-03 land.

The commodity name is the only tier-carrying key the balance has, so the tiers
belong on the commodity:

```{r commodity-tiers}
LAND <- newCommodity(
  name = "LAND",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "kha",
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), order = 1:3)
)
RES_LAND <- newSupply(
  name = "RES_LAND",
  commodity = "LAND",
  cluster = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    region = NA_character_,
    order = 1:3
  ),
  supply = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    ava.up = 4,              # kha available per grade
    cost = c(1, 2, 3)        # MUSD/kha
  )
)
EWIN_L <- newTechnology(
  name = "EWIN",
  input = data.frame(comm = "LAND", unit = "kha"),
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), region = NA_character_),
  ceff = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", "03"),
    comm = "ELC",
    cact2cout = c(1, 0.8, 0.5)
  ),
  capacity = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), cap.up = 100),
  invcost = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), invcost = 0.1),
  vintage = data.frame(olife = 30L),
  cap2act = 1
)
DEM_LAND <- newDemand(
  name = "DEM_ELC",
  commodity = "ELC",
  demand = data.frame(demand = 3)
)

repo_land <- newRepository(
  name = "repo_land",
  ELC, IMP_ELC, DEM_LAND, LAND, RES_LAND, EWIN_L
)
mod_land <- newModel(
  name = "art_land",
  repo = repo_land,
  calendar = cal,
  region = "R1",
  horizon = newHorizon(c(2025, 2030)),
  discount = 0.05
)
scen_land <- solve_model(
  obj = mod_land,
  name = "art_land",
  ondisk = FALSE,
  overwrite = TRUE,
  echo = FALSE
)

# one declaration, three commodities -- and one supply object, three processes
ava <- getData(scen_land, name = "pSupAva", merge = TRUE)
ava <- as.data.frame(ava)
unique(ava[, c("sup", "comm", "cluster")])
```

One declaration became three commodities, each with its own balance. The supply
object likewise became one process per tier, and every tier draws only its own:

```{r commodity-draw}
inp <- getData(scen_land, name = "vTechInp", merge = TRUE)
aggregate(value ~ tech + comm, inp, sum)   # kha
```

`EWIN_CL01` exhausts `LAND_CL01` and `EWIN_CL02` starts on `LAND_CL02`; no
variant ever touches another tier's land. The bound bites where you declared it,
from **one** commodity and **one** supply object -- which matters because
`supply@commodity` is a single name, so without tiered commodities a tier set
means one supply object per tier.

`ELC` in the same model has no clusters and is therefore shared by every
variant, with no flag anywhere. That is the rule in general: **tiering is opt-in
on the resource**, and a reference to an unclustered object is left alone.

## Tiers that differ in data, not just in name

Land tiers differ only in how much there is. Fuel grades differ in *what they
are*: anthracite and lignite are the same commodity in a model's structure and
not at all the same in carbon content. So `@emis`, `@agg` and `@property` carry
a `cluster` column too, with the broadcast rule you have seen everywhere else --
a row with no cluster is shared by every tier:

```{r coal-tiers}
COA <- newCommodity(
  name = "COA",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "PJ",
  cluster = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02"),
    desc = c("anthracite", "lignite"),
    order = 1:2
  ),
  emis = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02", NA),        # NA: the last row is shared
    comm    = c("CO2", "CO2", "SO2"),
    emis    = c(0.090, 0.110, 0.001)    # kt per PJ; 02 is the dirtier grade
  )
)
CO2 <- newCommodity(
  name = "CO2",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "kt",
  limtype = "UP"
)
SO2 <- newCommodity(
  name = "SO2",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "kt",
  limtype = "UP"
)
SUP_COA <- newSupply(
  name = "SUP_COA",
  commodity = "COA",
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), region = NA_character_),
  supply = data.frame(
    cluster = c("01", "02"),
    ava.up = 100,
    cost = c(3, 1)        # the dirty grade is the cheap one
  )
)
PP_COA <- newTechnology(
  name = "PP_COA",
  input = data.frame(comm = "COA", unit = "PJ"),
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), region = NA_character_),
  ceff = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), comm = "ELC", cact2cout = 0.4),
  capacity = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), cap.up = 100),
  invcost = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02"), invcost = 1),
  vintage = data.frame(olife = 30L),
  cap2act = 1
)

repo_coal <- newRepository(
  name = "repo_coal",
  ELC, CO2, SO2, IMP_ELC, DEM_LAND, COA, SUP_COA, PP_COA
)
mod_coal <- newModel(
  name = "art_coal",
  repo = repo_coal,
  calendar = cal,
  region = "R1",
  horizon = newHorizon(c(2025, 2030)),
  discount = 0.05
)
scen_coal <- interpolate_model(mod_coal, name = "art_coal", ondisk = FALSE)

ef <- getData(scen_coal, name = "pEmissionFactor", merge = TRUE)
ef <- as.data.frame(ef)
ef[, c("comm", "commp", "value")]   # kt per PJ
```

Each grade carries its own CO2 factor and both inherit the one shared SO2 row.
A grade is now a genuinely different fuel: cheap lignite with a high carbon
factor against costlier anthracite, and a CO2 cap decides which one runs.

Declared labels are authoritative here too, and the declaration is required: a
label that appears in a data slot but not in the `cluster` roster is a typo and
an error, and so is a data slot carrying labels with no roster at all. The
alternative -- harvesting the labels -- made a silent extra grade out of one
stray row.

# Reading a family back

Four calls, in increasing order of aggregation:

```{r reading, eval = FALSE}
getVariants(scen)                                  # the provenance table
getVariants(scen, class = "technology")             # one class
getData(scen, name = "vTechCap", variants = TRUE)   # results + provenance
variantSummary(scen, name = "vTechCap", by = "cluster")  # folded on one axis
```

`getData(..., variants = TRUE)` adds the provenance columns to the results,
which is usually what you want for plotting: group by `base` to draw the family,
by `cluster` to compare grades.

# Pitfalls

**The roster is required, on both axes.** A `cluster` or `vintage` label used
in any data slot must appear in `@cluster` / `@vintage`, or the object is
refused -- the error names the labels, the slots they came from, and the
declaration to paste. The roster is the authoritative set, so a misspelling is a
typo rather than an extra member built with defaults for everything it does not
carry (no investment cost, no capacity bound: free and unlimited). It is also
the only place `region` and `order` can be stated.

**A tier roster must cover what the processes ask for.** The consumer decides
which tiers exist; a process asking a clustered weather or commodity for a tier
it does not declare is an error naming both sides. The reverse is allowed: a
declared tier nobody references is still materialized, so its data stays
inspectable rather than vanishing.

**"Cluster" means something else in region aggregation.** In
`aggregate_model_regions(clusters = )` a cluster is a *group of regions* being
merged -- see the multi-level region article. The two never interact; the
collision is only in the English word.

**Names are data.** A member's name is a solver set member, so renaming
`variant_prefix` mid-project changes every result label, every levy target and
every golden. Pick it once per model.
